raw_response:
My land here in Quzhou is about 8 mu. I've been farming this same ground for over forty years. My father farmed it before me. I know this soil — it's sandy loam, drains reasonably well, but it gets dry fast in spring without irrigation. The water table has dropped some over the years, but I can still pump.

I'm not going to try anything new at my age. I've seen neighbors chase cotton, try vegetables, experiment with things. Some years they do better than me, some years they're wiped out. I can't afford to be wiped out. My son works in the city. I manage this land mostly myself now, with my wife helping at planting and harvest. I have to keep it manageable.

The answer is always the same: **winter wheat, then summer maize**. Wheat in, maize after. That's what this land is for. The local grain station buys it. I know the price, I know the costs, I know what yield to expect. The rotation is good for the soil too — keeps the weeds from getting too bad.

For wheat, I'll use the improved Jimai variety the county extension office has been promoting for several years now — not the newest one, the one that's been proven here. I know it handles rust and doesn't lodge when I fertilize. I'll plough before planting, apply compound fertilizer as base, topdress nitrogen at jointing. Three irrigations: one at sowing since it's been dry, one at jointing, one at heading. I'll spray herbicide once in winter and do one fungicide pass in spring before heading.

For maize after wheat harvest, I go quick. I use rotary tillage — no time to plough, and the rotary is easier on my back. I plant Zhengdan 958, it's reliable. I'll apply urea in two passes. Maize doesn't need as much irrigation if the summer rains come, but I'll be ready to pump twice if needed. One pesticide spray — mostly for fall armyworm and aphids.

I plough before wheat to manage residue and switch to rotary tillage for maize to turn the field around quickly after harvest.
